column4: The section's quoted ḥarth (tilth) divides seeking the Hereafter, whose field is increased, from seeking this world's field, which yields only a portion and no afterlife share; intention determines what kind of harvest endures.
The section says the purified share is the crop's due; this ayah commands giving the crop's حق on its harvest day, making the right part of the field's yield.
The section names the root خ ر ج for what emerges and explains tazkiya as giving from produce; this ayah joins spending good things to what God brought forth from earth.
The section's root ز ك و includes charity and purification; this ayah pairs sadaqa from wealth with cleansing and growth, making the share itself both purifying and increasing.
The section connects أفلح to staying in good and تَزَكَّىٰ to purification and growth; this ayah joins success to the soul's purification, showing the field image's inner outcome.
The section says growth can be suppressed like a seed buried in soil; this ayah's contrasting failure belongs to the one who دسّاها, burying or suppressing the soul, the inverse of cultivation.
The section's lexicon defines ف ل ح as splitting earth for tillage; this ayah says God splits the earth, the precise soil action that makes the field image visible.
The section frames purification through crop growth; this ayah's preceding rain poured abundantly supplies the water for the earth-splitting and food sequence that follows.
The section makes a field's yield an object of reflection; this ayah opens the neighboring sequence by telling the human to look at food, whose production the next ayat stage.
The section traces tilled soil into growing yield; this next ayah names grain as the first produce after the earth is split.
The section develops the field's growing products; this ayah continues the food sequence with grapes.
The section develops the field's growing products; this ayah continues the food sequence with olives.
The section develops the field's growing products; this ayah continues the food sequence with date palms.
The section develops the field's produce and pasture; this ayah adds dense gardens to the sequence.
The section ties field output to human use; this ayah completes the food sequence by calling the produce provision for people and their livestock.
The section's field image turns success into tilling and growth; this ayah asks whether people have considered what they sow, placing their work beside God's control of the crop.
The section contrasts a cultivated yield with pasture that dries and is swept away; this ayah says God could make what people cultivate into حطام, crop debris, the field's failed alternative.
The section's field scene moves from sowing to growth; this neighboring ayah says God is the one who makes the crop grow, completing the sowing question in 56:63.
After the crop could become debris in 56:65, this ayah gives the cultivators' imagined response that they would be burdened by loss; it sharpens the material cost of a ruined yield.
This neighboring ayah completes the crop-loss scenario with deprivation, contrasting the section's field whose due is paid from an actual yield.
The section rests on 87:4's أَخْرَجَ ٱلْمَرْعَىٰ and names the root خ ر ج; this ayah uses أَخْرَجَ for bringing out water and pasture, directly staging the same emergence of fodder.
The section treats pasture and crop as sustenance whose yield matters; this ayah completes the preceding pasture scene by calling it provision for people and their livestock.

The section's dictionary gloss for the remaining yield links success to what is preserved; Joseph tells the people to sow, harvest, and leave most grain in its ears, a measured reserve carried through future years.
The section contrasts a crop that is harvested and its due paid with vegetation lost; this ayah's coming drought consumes stored produce except a little kept, showing why measured remainder matters.
This ayah follows the years of stored grain with a year of rain and pressing produce; the sequence completes the section's account of crop output across measured seasons.
The section explicitly speaks of the crop's right on harvest day; these garden owners set out early to cut its fruit, placing the harvest at the center of their plan.
The section says the crop's due is to be given; the garden owners instead resolve that no poor person should enter, a direct withholding of the yield's rightful share.
The section contrasts productive cultivation with growth that dries and is swept away; the garden owners wake to find their crop blackened, the reversal of a harvestable field.

The section's harvest image is a managed field and its yield; this neighboring story begins with owners of a garden planning to harvest it in the morning, supplying the setting for their later refusal of the poor.
After discovering their ruined garden, the owners recognize they were deprived; this completes the contrast between a rightly shared yield and a harvest lost after withholding its share.
The section glosses تَزَكَّىٰ as giving charity from one's property; this ayah names the person who gives his wealth in order to purify himself, joining the same act to its inner aim.

The section relates crop growth to أَخْرَجَ and to 87:2's root س و ي for being set right; this ayah depicts a crop sending out its shoot, strengthening, thickening, and standing upright, a sustained growth rather than dried pasture.
The section explains تَزَكَّىٰ through purification and giving; this ayah calls the gardens' reward for one who purifies himself, linking the field's inward work to lasting recompense.
The section's root ف ل ح has the success sense of remaining in good; this ayah uses أَفْلَحَ for the believers, giving the field's agricultural word its Quranic success sense.
The section explains ز ك و as growth, charity, and purification; this ayah names those who perform zakat among the successful believers, joining the crop's given share to success.

The section connects giving zakat to success and what remains; this ayah pairs belief, prayer, and zakat with reward from the Lord and freedom from fear, linking the given share to enduring recompense.
The section links success to what remains in good; this continuation says the successful inherit Firdaws and abide there, specifying the lasting outcome of 23:1's success.
The section's ز ك و includes growth and an apportioned gift; this ayah compares spending in God's way to a grain producing seven ears, making giving and multiplying harvest one image.
The section joins giving a share to blessed growth; this ayah pictures those who spend seeking God's approval as a garden on fertile ground that yields double after rain.

The section's root ز ك و includes growth and charity; this ayah contrasts God erasing usury with making charities grow, clarifying the difference between increase by taking and increase through giving.
The section links ز ك و to growth and paying a share; this ayah contrasts wealth lent for increase with zakat given seeking God's face, whose givers are multiplied.

The section says a rightful portion is given from the yield; this ayah commands giving relatives, the needy, and travelers their due, making the harvest's share part of a broader obligation to distribute wealth.
The section describes purification through a property share; this ayah tells the hearer to give relatives, needy people, and travelers their حق, the due portion associated with material provision.
The section's crop has a right that is paid; this ayah says a recognized حق in the believers' wealth belongs to the asker and deprived, specifying recipients for a share.
The section says the product's right is to be paid; this ayah describes a prescribed right in wealth, making the share a defined portion rather than whatever remains by chance.
This continuation identifies the prescribed right's recipients as the asker and deprived, completing 70:24's account of a due in wealth.
The section's field is purified when its rightful share is paid; this ayah condemns hoarding gold and silver without spending in God's way, the opposite treatment of wealth.
This continuation describes the consequence of hoarding by using heated treasure to brand its possessors, completing 9:34's warning against withholding wealth's due.

The section links a property share to success; this ayah praises preferring others despite one's own need and says those guarded from stinginess are successful, giving the share a concrete ethical form.

The section contrasts neighboring ground with different fates; this ayah explicitly describes adjacent plots, watered alike yet differing in yield, so cultivation's outcome is not reducible to shared soil.
The section's pasture is a crop that serves living creatures; this ayah gives rain to drink and trees in which livestock graze, supplying the water and fodder around the cultivated scene.
This continuation says rain grows crops, olives, dates, grapes, and fruits; it expands the section's field image into varied yield.
The section treats cultivated ground as a source of yield; this ayah says earth is laid out for creatures, introducing a sequence of fruits, grain, and produce.
The sequence names fruit and date palms with sheathed clusters, specifying the field's edible yield.
This continuation names grain with husk and aromatic plants, extending the produce scene into grain and fodder.
The section describes grain growing from split earth; this ayah stages rain producing green growth, grain, dates, grapes, olives, and pomegranates, making divine provision visible in harvest.

The section's root ر ب ب is glossed as tending a farm; this ayah presents God making earth a dwelling, sending water, and bringing forth varied plants, framing the cultivated land as sustained provision.
The section connects growth to products for use; this continuation tells people to eat and pasture livestock, completing the plant scene with its human and animal yield.
The section's field begins with growth from earth; this ayah calls dead earth a sign when revived and producing grain people eat.
This continuation adds date and grape gardens with springs to the grain scene, extending the field's growth into sustained fruit-bearing cultivation.
The continuation connects garden fruit to eating and provision; this completes the crop sequence with the yield that the section treats as a shareable product.
The section links pasture and crop to provision; this ayah describes water driven to barren land, crops grown for people and livestock, directly joining soil growth to use.
The section's field depends on growth after water; this ayah sends rain-bearing clouds to dead land and brings out fruits, connecting earth's revival to produce.
The section makes ز ك و an image of growth; this ayah describes dead earth stirring, swelling, and producing varied growth after rain, a close parallel for emergence from soil.
The section traces land from growth toward yield; this ayah asks the reader to look at the fruits of God's mercy as he revives the earth after its death.
The section's crop depends on earth that can be made productive; this ayah describes humbled earth that revives and grows after water is sent down.
The section develops measured growth into yield; this ayah pairs blessed rain with gardens and grain for harvest, showing the field's fruit as provision.
This continuation adds tall date palms with clustered fruit, another concrete yield from the water-grown landscape.
The sequence names provision for servants and the reviving of dead land; it completes the crop scene by connecting field growth to sustenance.
The section's crop requires water for growth; this ayah sends abundant water from clouds as the opening of a sequence about grain and gardens.
This continuation says the rain brings forth grain and plants, directly naming the field's products.
The sequence ends in thick gardens, completing the growth from water through crop to cultivated abundance.

The section's dictionary gloss of harvest yield includes a known measure; this ayah says water is sent down by measure, lodged in earth, and can be taken away, making provision measured and contingent.
After measured water, this ayah gives gardens of dates and grapes as food, a concrete result of the provision described in 23:18.
This continuation names the olive tree and its oil and condiment, extending the garden's produce into usable yield.
The section moves from growth to a crop's measured yield; this ayah says God sends water in measure, revives dead land, and brings people forth likewise, joining measurement, soil, and growth.
The section's roots connect growth to staying in good; this ayah compares a good word to a sound tree, giving the image a rooted form of enduring growth.
This continuation says the tree yields fruit every season by its Lord's leave, directly joining growth to recurring yield and divine care.
The contrast is a bad tree uprooted from the earth with no stability, the opposite of the section's tended crop that grows and remains fruitful.
The section says pasture can dry and be carried away; this ayah likens worldly life to rain-grown plants that become harvested down as if absent the day before, making apparent flourishing transient.
The section contrasts cultivated growth with vegetation that dries and is swept off; this ayah says rain-grown plants become dry stubble scattered by winds, directly staging that fate.
The section traces growth toward a lasting good; this ayah shows crops grow, yellow, and become debris, a direct scene of what passes rather than remains.
The section contrasts durable success with pasture that withers; this ayah's rain-grown vegetation yellows and becomes chaff within its account of worldly life's brief display.

The section contrasts what the flood carries away with a productive yield that remains; this ayah's flood carries foam off while what benefits people stays on earth, clarifying the difference between passing residue and lasting use.
The section joins a paid share to what lasts; this ayah calls wealth and children worldly adornment but says enduring righteous deeds are better in reward and hope.
The section's root ب ق ي names both harvest remainder and what endures; this ayah contrasts what people have that perishes with what is with God that remains.

The section reads the field's successful remainder alongside 87:17's better and more abiding Hereafter; this ayah directly contrasts worldly provision with what is with God, which is better and more lasting.
The section connects success to lasting good; this ayah calls worldly life a passing enjoyment and the Hereafter the abode of permanence, defining what remains beyond the crop's season.
